passages.label: READING PASSAGE 1
passages.instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.
passages.title: The Environmental Cost of Consumer Goods
passages.subtitle: Unpacking the ecological footprint of fast fashion, e-commerce packaging, and short-lived electronics
paragraphs: Modern retail thrives on speed and abundance. Automated mass production and ultra-fast global shipping have driven down prices for clothing, homeware, and digital gadgets, fuelling a culture of relentless consumerism. While affordable goods have raised material comfort for billions, environmental auditors calculate that household consumption accounts for roughly two-thirds of global greenhouse gas emissions once full supply chains are measured.

Every purchased item carries a hidden carbon footprint—spanning raw-material mining, factory energy, international freight, and eventual disposal. The fast-fashion sector illustrates this strain vividly. To release micro-trends every fortnight, brands rely heavily on synthetic polyester spun from crude oil, alongside water-intensive cotton farming and toxic fabric bleaches. Millions of tonnes of lightly worn garments are incinerated or shipped to overseas landfills each year.

Convenience culture has also multiplied disposable products and multi-layered packaging. Coffee cups lined with thin plastic waterproof film cannot be recycled in ordinary paper mills, while the boom in next-day e-commerce has filled domestic bins with air pillows, tape, and oversized cartons designed to protect single lightweight items during rough van deliveries.

Even durable household appliances often suffer from planned obsolescence. Consumer groups complain that smartphones, headphones, and dishwashers are routinely engineered with sealed batteries, proprietary screws, or software updates that slow older chips—encouraging replacement every two or three years rather than straightforward repair. As a result, electronic waste ('e-waste') is now the fastest-growing domestic waste stream on Earth.

Pushback is gaining momentum through both ethical consumption and smart regulation. Shoppers increasingly turn to resale platforms, refill grocery stations, and neighbourhood 'libraries of things' where residents borrow drills or camping tents instead of buying them. On the legal front, France has introduced a mandatory 'repairability index' printed on electronics boxes, scoring devices from one to ten so buyers can reward manufacturers who design products built to last.

passages.label: READING PASSAGE 2
passages.instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.
passages.title: From Fossil Fuels to Renewable Energy
passages.subtitle: Evaluating the economics, intermittency challenges, and geopolitical rewards of clean power
paragraphs: A Coal, oil, and natural gas—collectively termed fossil fuels—powered two centuries of industrial transformation. Because these underground deposits formed over geological timescales, they are strictly non-renewable. More pressingly, combusting them drives both urban air toxicity and climate instability, compelling governments worldwide to accelerate the transition toward renewable energy.

B Solar and wind power now lead global capacity additions by a wide margin. Unlike coal or gas stations that require continuous fuel shipments and emit heavy carbon dioxide, wind turbines and photovoltaic panels generate zero-emission electricity using free natural flows. Once installed, their marginal operating expenses are minimal, allowing clean plants to deliver predictable power prices for twenty-five to thirty years.

C Beyond climate goals, renewables strengthen national energy security. Countries that import most of their oil and liquefied gas remain acutely exposed to foreign conflicts, pipeline disruptions, and sudden price spikes that squeeze both factories and household budgets. Harnessing domestic sunlight, offshore winds, and geothermal heat enables governments to reduce dependence on volatile international fuel markets.

D Nevertheless, replacing fossil fuels on a national scale poses formidable engineering and financial hurdles. First, constructing offshore wind arrays, modernising ageing transmission cables, and training technicians demand a massive initial investment long before revenues arrive. Second, solar and wind suffer from 'intermittency'—output falls sharply at night or during windless winter high-pressure spells—creating the risk of blackouts unless backup capacity is always available.

E Grid engineers are deploying an array of innovations to solve intermittency. Utility-scale batteries, pumped-hydro reservoirs that store water uphill during sunny hours, and 'green hydrogen' produced from surplus wind power can all release electricity when skies darken. In parallel, smart meters encourage households to charge electric cars overnight when wind generation is abundant and tariffs drop.

F Economic trends increasingly favour the clean transition: utility-scale solar electricity has plunged in cost by nearly ninety percent since 2010, making it the cheapest new power source in most regions. Analysts conclude that while grid upgrades require bold upfront funding, the long-term payoff is a cleaner, self-reliant energy system.

passages.label: READING PASSAGE 3
passages.instruction: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.
passages.title: Oil and Gas in Untouched Wilderness
passages.subtitle: Debating resource extraction across polar tundras, deep rainforests, and fragile marine frontiers
paragraphs: 1 Despite rapid expansion in renewable power, global energy demand remains closely tied to petroleum and natural gas for aviation, shipping, and chemical manufacturing. As easily accessible reserves in older basins decline, multinational energy corporations are pushing into remote ecological frontiers—from Arctic permafrost plains to unlogged Amazonian basins. Whether drilling should be permitted inside an untouched wilderness has become a defining clash between short-term economic gain and irreversible environmental loss.

2 Proponents of frontier extraction frame the issue around affordability and regional development. Expanding domestic oil and gas supply, they argue, shields consumers from volatile fuel imports, generates royalties for state budgets, and brings high-wage technical jobs to isolated northern or jungle municipalities. Industry engineers further contend that directional drilling—which taps multiple underground pockets from a single small gravel pad—dramatically shrinks the surface footprint compared with twentieth-century oil fields.

3 Conservation biologists counter that 'smaller footprint' claims disguise wider disruption. Opening a pristine environment requires access highways, seismic blasting lines, pipelines, and airstrips that slice continuous landscapes into fragments. This habitat destruction blocks seasonal caribou migrations, exposes previously unreachable rainforests to illegal loggers and poachers, and accelerates thawing of carbon-rich permafrost beneath heated pipelines.

4 The spectre of a catastrophic oil spill magnifies these concerns. In ice-choked polar seas or dense equatorial rivers, sub-zero storms, winter darkness, and vast distances from emergency ports render rapid containment nearly impossible. Experience from past maritime and jungle leaks demonstrates that heavy crude lingers beneath ice floes and river sediment for decades, inflicting severe ecological damage on seabirds, fish spawning grounds, and local subsistence fisheries.

5 Indigenous communities residing in these regions raise profound questions of justice. Having stewarded wild ecosystems sustainably for millennia, many argue they are rarely given genuine veto power over national drilling licences. While corporate revenues flow largely to distant shareholders and capital cities, local villages absorb contaminated groundwater, noise pollution, and the erosion of traditional livelihoods.

6 In my judgment, sacrificing the planet's last intact wildernesses for new fossil reserves is both ecologically reckless and economically short-sighted. Global climate agencies already warn that meeting international warming limits leaves no room for developing untouched oil fields. Redirecting those billions toward grid storage, public transit, and community-led conservation protects biodiversity while building a far more durable future.
